exercise_group.instruction: In Exercises 1–4, the matrix $$A$$ is followed by a sequence $$\{\textbf{x}_{k}\}$$ produced by the power method. Use these data to estimate the largest eigenvalue of $$A$$ , and give a corresponding eigenvector.

problem.paragraph: Find a vector with a $$1$$ in the second entry that is close to an eigenvector of $$A$$ . Use four decimal places. Check your estimate, and give an estimate for the dominant eigenvalue of $$A$$ .

Let $$A = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{rr} {- 2} & {- 3} \\ 6 & 7 \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ . Repeat Exercise 5, using the following sequence $$\textbf{x},A\textbf{x},\ldots,A^{5}\textbf{x}$$ . $$\begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} , \begin{bmatrix} - 5 \\ 13 \end{bmatrix} , \begin{bmatrix} - 29 \\ 61 \end{bmatrix} , \begin{bmatrix} - 125 \\ 253 \end{bmatrix} , \begin{bmatrix} - 509 \\ 1021 \end{bmatrix} , \begin{bmatrix} - 2045 \\ 4093 \end{bmatrix}$$

exercise_group.instruction: Exercises 7–12 require MATLAB or other computational aid. In Exercises 7 and 8, use the power method with the $$\textbf{x}_{0}$$ given. List $$\{\textbf{x}_{k}\}$$ and $$\{\mu_{k}\}$$ for $$k = 1,\ldots,5$$ . In Exercises 9 and 10, list $$\mu_{5}$$ and $$\mu_{6}$$ .

Another estimate can be made for an eigenvalue when an approximate eigenvector is available. Observe that if $$A\textbf{x} = \text{λ} \textbf{x}$$ , then $$\textbf{x}^{T}A\textbf{x} = \textbf{x}^{T}( \text{λ} \textbf{x}) = \text{λ} (\textbf{x}^{T}\textbf{x})$$ , and the Rayleigh quotient﻿

equals $$\text{λ}$$ . If $$\textbf{x}$$ is close to an eigenvector for $$\text{λ}$$ , then this quotient is close to $$\text{λ}$$ . When $$A$$ is a symmetric matrix $$(A^{T} = A)$$ , the Rayleigh quotient $$R(\textbf{x}_{k}) = (\textbf{x}_{k}^{T} A\textbf{x}_{k})/(\textbf{x}_{k}^{T}\textbf{x}_{k})$$ will have roughly twice as many digits of accuracy as the scaling factor $$\mu_{k}$$ in the power method. Verify this increased accuracy in Exercises 11 and 12 by computing $$\mu_{k}$$ and $$R(\textbf{x}_{k})$$ for $$k = 1,\ldots,4$$ .
Exercises 13 and 14 apply to a $$3 \times 3$$ matrix $$A$$ whose eigenvalues are estimated to be $$4$$ , $$- 4$$ , and $$3$$ .

problem.paragraph: If the eigenvalues close to $$4$$ and $$- 4$$ are known to have different absolute values, will the power method work? Is it likely to be useful?
Suppose the eigenvalues close to $$4$$ and $$- 4$$ are known to have exactly the same absolute value. Describe how one might obtain a sequence that estimates the eigenvalue close to $$4 .$$

Suppose $$A\textbf{x} = \text{λ} \textbf{x}$$ with $$\textbf{x} \neq \textbf{0}$$ . Let $$\alpha$$ be a scalar different from the eigenvalues of $$A$$ , and let $$B = (A - \alpha I)^{- 1}$$ . Subtract $$\alpha\textbf{x}$$ from both sides of the equation $$A\textbf{x} = \text{λ} \textbf{x}$$ , and use algebra to show that $$1/( \text{λ} - \alpha)$$ is an eigenvalue of $$B$$ , with $$\textbf{x}$$ a corresponding eigenvector.

Suppose $$\mu$$ is an eigenvalue of the $$B$$ in Exercise 15, and that $$\textbf{x}$$ is a corresponding eigenvector, so that $$(A - \alpha I)^{- 1}\textbf{x} = \mu\textbf{x}$$ . Use this equation to find an eigenvalue of $$A$$ in terms of $$\mu$$ and $$\alpha$$ . [Note: $$\mu \neq 0$$ because $$B$$ is invertible.]
[T] Use the inverse power method to estimate the middle eigenvalue of the $$A$$ in Example 3, with accuracy to four decimal places. Set $$\textbf{x}_{0} = (1,0,0)$$ .

[T] Let $$A$$ be as in Exercise 9. Use the inverse power method with $$\textbf{x}_{0} = (1,0,0)$$ to estimate the eigenvalue of $$A$$ near $$\alpha = - 1.4$$ , with an accuracy to four decimal places.

exercise_group.instruction: In Exercises 19 and 20, find (a) the largest eigenvalue and (b) the eigenvalue closest to zero. In each case, set $$\textbf{x}_{0} = (1,0,0,0)$$ and carry out approximations until the approximating sequence seems accurate to four decimal places. Include the approximate eigenvector.

problem.paragraph: A common misconception is that if $$A$$ has a strictly dominant eigenvalue, then, for any sufficiently large value of $$k$$ , the vector $$A^{k}\textbf{x}$$ is approximately equal to an eigenvector of $$A$$ . For the three matrices below, study what happens to $$A^{k}\textbf{x}$$ when $$\textbf{x} = (.5,.5)$$ , and try to draw general conclusions (for a $$2 \times 2$$ matrix).

list.item: If $$A\textbf{x}$$ is nearly a multiple of $$\textbf{x}$$ , then the ratios of corresponding entries in the two vectors should be nearly constant. So compute: $$\begin{matrix}\left{ \text{entry} \text{in} A \mathbf{x}\right} & \div & \left{ \text{entry} \text{in} \mathbf{x}\right} & = & \left{ \text{ratio} \right}\end{matrix} \begin{matrix}3.00 & & 1.00 & & 3.000 \\ - 13.00 & & - 4.30 & & 3.023 \\ 24.50 & & 8.10 & & 3.025\end{matrix}$$

Each entry in $$A\textbf{x}$$ is about $$3$$ times the corresponding entry in $$\textbf{x}$$ , so $$\textbf{x}$$ is close to an eigenvector. Any of the ratios above is an estimate for the eigenvalue. (To five decimal places, the eigenvalue is $$3.02409$$ .)
